name: The Company’s guns at Idah

summary.text: The Royal Niger Company, chartered in 1886, set up trading posts at Idah and along the river. Prince Akwu led a guerrilla war against the Company, raiding its stores at Idah several times, and the Company answered by shelling Idah from the river: in 1896, the bombardment with which a recent history dates the subjugation of Igalaland, and by one account again before 1900. Attah Amaga died in February 1900 and with him Igala’s independence. The British installed Attah Ocheje Onokpa in 1901, then deposed him in 1903 and banished him to Asaba, where he died.

routes.label: 1903: Attah Ocheje Onokpa banished to Asaba
1903: Adukwu Okekwu exiled to Old Calabar

moments.title: Prince Akwu’s raids
moments.text: Akwu and his followers raid the Company’s stores at Idah several times and attack European traders on the river.

moments.title: Idah bombarded
moments.text: The Company shells Idah from a vessel on the Niger. Igala memory recalls the palace as the target and the town emptied as people fled inland.

moments.title: The end of independence
moments.text: Attah Amaga dies. Britain has proclaimed its protectorates the month before, and Igala’s independence ends with him.

moments.title: Adukwu Okekwu’s attack
moments.text: Adukwu Okekwu attacks the assistant district commissioner, Boyle, and his escort near Alade. He is captured, tried and exiled to Old Calabar, where he dies.

note: Ineke (2025) dates the bombardment to 1896; James (2017) has two between 1896 and 1900. Ineke was read only in a search extract.
reviewNotes: The owner asked to show when Idah was attacked by the British. Written sources found give only “twice between 1896 and 1900” (James 2017). One web summary lists bombardments in 1822, 1879, 1882, 1896 and 1900, with no source. Which attacks does the owner know of, and from which book, archive or elders?
The Prince is called Akwu Amaga in one version and Akwu Agahiu in another.
